## Logits and softmax

The last layer of the network emits one real number — a **logit** $z_i$ —
for every token in the vocabulary. Softmax turns those logits into a
probability distribution:

$$
p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} \exp(z_j / T)}
$$

Softmax uses the **same probability mapping** as multinomial or
conditional logit — the language model as a whole should not be described
as a multinomial-logit model; only this final mapping shares that
functional form. For fixed logits, the algebraic odds-ratio property
associated with IIA survives; it carries no behavioral or welfare
reading here. <span class="cite">[S-01] [S-02] [S-03] &middot; 3B1B ch.5, 22:22</span>
<span class="timing">2.5 min &middot; cum. 2.5</span>

::: {.notes}
Running example for this and the next two slides: "Given the traffic
data, the agency decided to ___ the bridge," with five candidate
continuations — repair, monitor, replace, close, ignore — and logits
(2.0, 1.0, 0.5, −0.5, −3.0). This is the same example used in
`learn/softmax-sampling.qmd` and its live interactive.

Say explicitly: the resemblance to multinomial logit is in the
*arithmetic* of the mapping, not in the *econometrics* — $z_i$ is not a
linear index in observed covariates, it is the output of a deep,
context-dependent network. Full treatment, including where the analogy
breaks down, is on the website module linked at the end of the next
slide's section.

Target: 2.5 minutes for this slide.
:::

## Training and maximum likelihood

At each token position, the model defines a categorical probability
distribution through softmax. Training maximizes the conditional
likelihood of the observed next tokens across the corpus — equivalently,
it minimizes negative log likelihood (cross-entropy):

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

This is maximum-likelihood training, but it is not a conventional
econometric exercise aimed at identifying interpretable structural
parameters or reporting classical standard errors.
<span class="cite">[S-05] [S-06] &middot; Karpathy, 20:11</span>
<span class="timing">2.5 min &middot; cum. 5.0</span>

::: {.notes}
Do not imply that uncertainty measures are mathematically impossible —
only that this is not the kind of estimation exercise that reports them
by default. Optimization mechanics (gradient descent, backpropagation)
are intentionally out of scope for this vertical slice; they belong to a
later module (`learn/training.qmd`, not yet built) and a later slide in
the full deck.

Target: 2.5 minutes for this slide. Cumulative so far: 5.0 minutes.
:::

## Sampling and temperature

Temperature $T$ rescales every logit before the softmax normalization is
applied.

- **Argmax is deterministic and introduces no sampling variation; sampling
  can produce different continuations from the same probability
  distribution.**
- As $T \to 0$: the distribution converges to argmax.
- As $T \to \infty$: the distribution approaches uniform.

**Lowering the temperature does not make an answer more truthful.** The
training objective rewards plausible continuation, not verified truth —
deterministic decoding can be just as confidently wrong as sampling.
<span class="cite">[S-04] [S-07] &middot; 3B1B ch.5, 22:22 &middot; Karpathy, 26:01</span>
<span class="timing">2.5 min &middot; cum. 7.5</span>

The $T \to 0$ convergence to argmax assumes a unique highest logit; a
tie splits the limiting mass among the tied candidates. This
qualification is stated on the website module, not spoken live — say it
only if asked.
